item.content:encoded: Escambia County, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Images of the Cat in the Hat character being used to signal threats against schools have circulated in Escambia, Okaloosa, and possibly Santa Rosa counties in recent days. Officials say the meme is being treated as a credible threat indicator whenever it appears, even though no incidents have materialized locally. Deputies are reminding parents to talk with their kids about not sharing this kind of content, even as a joke, since it can trigger a major law enforcement and school security response regardless of intent.

item.title: UWF Students Help Wildlife Sanctuary Plan Relocation Campaign
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- University of West Florida marketing students conducted a professional-level feasibility study for the Wildlife Sanctuary of Northwest Florida, helping the organization plan a capital campaign to move out of a chronic flood zone. Students surveyed Escambia and Santa Rosa County residents, finding the community has…
item.content:encoded: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- University of West Florida marketing students conducted a professional-level feasibility study for the Wildlife Sanctuary of Northwest Florida, helping the organization plan a capital campaign to move out of a chronic flood zone. Students surveyed Escambia and Santa Rosa County residents, finding the community has the capacity to support the campaign, especially through emotional, animal-centered storytelling and targeting prior donors. Professor James Mead says the research would normally cost fifty-thousand dollars or more if done by a professional firm. The Wildlife Sanctuary has since launched its capital campaign and applied for additional grant funding to relocate to a new ten-acre campus.

item.content:encoded: A newly approved treatment is giving doctors another tool in fighting pancreatic cancer, one of the most difficult cancers to manage. According to WKRG News 5, the FDA approval represents a potentially significant step forward for patients facing this aggressive disease. Pancreatic cancer remains notoriously challenging to treat, with historically low survival rates compared to many other cancer types. The new option could expand the arsenal available to oncologists treating local patients diagnosed with the disease. For West Florida residents or their families dealing with a pancreatic cancer diagnosis, discussing this new treatment option with their medical team may be worthwhile. The development underscores ongoing efforts in the medical community to improve outcomes for one of cancer's most formidable opponents.

item.content:encoded:
Escambia County Sheriff's Office deputies have arrested a woman in connection with a homicide that occurred in August, according to officials. Ashanti Brown, 23, faces charges of homicide and tampering with evidence in the case.

The arrest follows an investigation by ECSO into the August homicide. Few additional details about the circumstances of the death or the investigation have been released at this time.

Brown remains in custody facing the two felony charges. Anyone with information about the case is encouraged to contact the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

item.content:encoded: A fire at Rocky Creek Baptist Church in George County, Mississippi has prompted an early dismissal at a nearby elementary school as firefighters battle the blaze. According to the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency, the church's activities building is fully engulfed in flames, with multiple fire departments responding to the scene. While the fire itself is in George County—outside the Pensacola area—the incident underscores how quickly emergency situations can affect school operations and surrounding communities. Officials have not yet released information on the cause of the fire or any injuries. The school's early dismissal was a precautionary measure as emergency crews worked to contain the flames.

item.title: Patronis pushes bill to rename Lake Ontario 'Lake America'

item.content:encoded: Congressman Jimmy Patronis has introduced legislation that would officially change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, according to WKRG News 5. The Florida Republican's Lake America Act would need to pass both chambers of Congress to become law. Lake Ontario is the smallest of the five Great Lakes and sits primarily on the U.S.-Canada border. The reasoning behind Patronis's proposal and its likelihood of passage remain unclear. If approved, it would represent a significant change to one of North America's most recognizable geographic features.

item.title: Escambia Sheriff Discusses Flock Camera Fallout, Murder Charge, and Vape Shop Burglaries
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons joined Pensacola's Morning News Tuesday with updates on several active cases, along with his agency's response to a state order that's forcing changes to its license plate reader program. Flock Cameras Simmons says Governor Ron DeSantis's order requiring the removal of automated license plate readers from state…
item.content:encoded:
Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons joined Pensacola's Morning News Tuesday with updates on several active cases, along with his agency's response to a state order that's forcing changes to its license plate reader program.


Flock Cameras

Simmons says Governor Ron DeSantis's order requiring the removal of automated license plate readers from state road rights-of-way is going to hit ECSO's network hard. He says roughly a third of the agency's cameras sit on state roads, and pulling them out will meaningfully weaken a system that depends on being complete to function well. The Florida Department of Transportation gave agencies 30 days to remove the cameras or have state crews do it for them.


Simmons says his cameras haven't been switched off yet and won't be used any less in the meantime — if a crime happens today and a license plate reader can help, his office is going to use it. But he says the agency is actively weighing whether to keep running a smaller, less effective network once the state road cameras come down, or pause the whole program until there's more legal clarity, an approach several other Florida sheriff's offices, including Duval, Volusia, and Seminole counties, have already taken.


Second-Degree Murder Charge

A woman told deputies she shot a man in self-defense during an incident at a Pine Forest Road apartment, but Simmons says the investigation didn't support her claim. Ashanti Brown is now charged with second-degree murder. Simmons says Brown allegedly took a doorbell camera and her cell phone from the scene and discarded them in a ditch in Santa Rosa County — a detail he says undercuts her account, since someone acting in self-defense would typically want that evidence reviewed, not hidden. Investigators are still working to access the data on the discarded devices. Simmons says the charge could be upgraded depending on what they find, though that would likely require evidence the shooting was planned or an ambush.


Vape Shop Burglaries

Deputies arrested three people in connection with five vape shop burglaries reported over the past couple weeks near Nine Mile Road. Simmons says vape shops and marijuana dispensaries have become a recent target locally, with burglars likely assuming the businesses keep cash or product on hand overnight. He says the arrests came after investigators worked the pattern of break-ins.


Other Cases

A 27-year-old man reported being shot in the calf near Wedgwood but refused to tell deputies what happened, leading Simmons to suspect the wound may have been self-inflicted. Simmons also addressed a Cat in the Hat meme circulating online that's being used to signal school threats, with incidents reported in Escambia, Okaloosa, and possibly Santa Rosa counties. He says no threats materialized locally, but his office treats every one seriously given the disruption and fear they can cause, even when they turn out to be a joke.

item.content:encoded: Santa Rosa County, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office is still searching for a suspect who vandalized Soundside High School last week, causing more than eleven-thousand dollars in damage. The August twenty-sixth vandalism, captured on the school's security cameras, damaged an exterior door and lock, brick fascia, and two trash cans, though nothing was taken. Superintendent Karen Barber says the district has confidence in the sheriff's ongoing investigation. Soundside, a two-hundred-fifty-thousand-square-foot facility, is the first new high school built in Santa Rosa County in thirty years and opened earlier this month.

item.content:encoded: Santa Rosa County Schools announced this week that it will increase law enforcement and security staff at its campuses in response to a viral social media challenge circulating online. The district issued a notice alerting families to the heightened presence of officers and security personnel as a precautionary measure. The "Cat in the Hat" trend, which has prompted similar responses from schools across the country, has raised concern among administrators about potential disruptions or safety issues on campus. The district did not provide specific details about the nature of the challenge or any incidents that may have occurred locally, but emphasized that the additional security is meant to ensure student and staff safety. Parents can expect to see more uniformed personnel in and around school buildings as the district works to monitor and address the situation.

item.title: Former Pensacola Contractor Jesse LaCoste Sentenced To 30 Additional Years In Prison
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Former Pensacola contractor Jesse LaCoste was sentenced Monday to thirty years in prison for racketeering and contractor fraud, a sentence that will be added on top of the ten years he's already serving from a separate case last year. The 34-year-old former contractor was found guilty Thursday on both charges. He…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Former Pensacola contractor Jesse LaCoste was sentenced Monday to thirty years in prison for racketeering and contractor fraud, a sentence that will be added on top of the ten years he's already serving from a separate case last year.

The 34-year-old former contractor was found guilty Thursday on both charges. He received thirty years for each, though the sentences will run concurrently. Judge John Simon also ordered LaCoste to pay more than two million dollars in restitution to his victims. LaCoste claims he has no funds or assets left to pay, saying the money he received from clients was reinvested back into his company for other projects.


LaCoste and his company were accused of starting construction jobs, collecting payment, and then never finishing the work. He took the stand for nearly half an hour Monday morning, asking the judge for mercy before learning his sentence. "I'm not trying to shift blame, I'm not trying to do any of those things," LaCoste said. "I'm only trying to show the intention of my heart."


He said he had been trying to build a business, take care of his family, and serve the Pensacola community. LaCoste pushed back against the words "scam" and "fraud" being used throughout the trial, saying he never intended to harm anyone and that he suffered alongside those affected.


Prosecutors painted a different picture. The state presented more than 40 witnesses and 70 pieces of evidence during trial, with several victims saying they lost their life savings paying LaCoste for work that was never completed. Assistant State Attorney Paul Gillespie said county records show that of 22 projects LaCoste took on for Escambia County, only four were ever finished, with several others plagued by failed inspections and missing permits.

"He took from nearly every walk of life," Gillespie said. "The elderly, the young, the professional, the everyday man, men, women, black, white, from every demographic of our community, including firefighters, veterans."


Several victims spoke during Monday's sentencing hearing. LaCoste's attorney had asked for the minimum sentence of 69 months.


"I do find that this was an egregious set of circumstances and acts for persons who trusted their builder and took their money and they never saw it again or the results of their labor," Judge Simon said.


Court records show LaCoste still faces additional charges in cases pending in Santa Rosa and Okaloosa counties.

item.title: Local Agencies Begin Complying With Order to Remove License Plate Readers From State Roads
item.dc:creator: news6334
item.description: Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Escambia and Okaloosa County law enforcement agencies say they'll comply with a Florida Department of Transportation order requiring automated license plate readers to come off state highways and rights-of-way within 30 days. Pensacola Police PIO Mike Wood says the department is still working out exactly how many…
item.content:encoded:
Pensacola, FL (NewsRadio 92.3) -- Escambia and Okaloosa County law enforcement agencies say they'll comply with a Florida Department of Transportation order requiring automated license plate readers to come off state highways and rights-of-way within 30 days. Pensacola Police PIO Mike Wood says the department is still working out exactly how many of its cameras sit on state road right-of-way.


"Now that we have 30 days to remove these cameras from state roadways, that's exactly what we're going to do," Wood told WEAR. He says cameras on local and county roads will keep running as long as they remain legal.


Escambia County Sheriff Chip Simmons tells NewsRadio that his agency is facing a bigger hit than most — roughly a third of ECSO's Flock cameras sit on state roadways, and he says pulling them will meaningfully weaken a network that depends on being complete to work well. Simmons says the agency hasn't shut any cameras off yet since it still has the full 30 days but is actively deciding whether to keep running a smaller, less effective system or pause the program entirely while the legal and legislative picture sorts itself out.


Okaloosa County Sheriff Eric Aden says his office will go further than the state order requires, removing cameras from county roads as well, even though FDOT's memo only covers state right-of-way. In a statement, Aden called the move disappointing from a public safety standpoint but said the agency will comply and revisit the technology later if clearer legal guidance emerges. The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office says it's reviewing its own ALPR program, citing the technology's track record in solving homicides and locating missing children and vulnerable adults, while acknowledging it needs to weigh that value against community privacy concerns.


The FDOT memo, signed by Chief Operating Officer Will Watts, revokes all general use permits previously issued to local law enforcement for camera placement in state right-of-way, citing concerns about rapid growth in the technology, data privacy, and surveillance. Agencies that don't remove their own cameras within 30 days will have them removed by FDOT crews.


Governor Ron DeSantis said Monday he supports giving law enforcement tools to investigate crime but doesn't want Florida becoming what he called a digital surveillance state, and says he's pushing for legislation to set clearer rules around the technology. Critics of the cameras, including Pensacola-based advocate Jacob Rockwell, call the state's action a step in the right direction and argue county governments should go further and ban the cameras from county roads as well.

item.title: Escambia County Felon Pleads Guilty to Federal Meth, Gun Charges
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A 26-year-old Escambia County man has admitted in federal court to drug trafficking and weapons violations, according to court records. Travis W. Carroll pleaded guilty to three federal counts: possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession of a firearm or ammunition as a convicted felon, and possession of a firearm in…
item.content:encoded:
A 26-year-old Escambia County man has admitted in federal court to drug trafficking and weapons violations, according to court records. Travis W. Carroll pleaded guilty to three federal counts: possession with intent to distribute methamphetamine, possession of a firearm or ammunition as a convicted felon, and possession of a firearm in furtherance of drug trafficking.

The guilty plea comes after federal authorities charged Carroll with combining criminal drug activity with illegal weapons possession—a combination that typically results in enhanced penalties under federal law. As a previously convicted felon, Carroll was prohibited from possessing firearms under federal statute, making the weapons charges particularly serious.

Carroll is scheduled for sentencing at a later date. Federal charges of this nature typically carry substantial prison time, especially when firearms are connected to drug distribution activity.

item.title: Florida Removes License Plate Reader Cameras From State Roads
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: Governor Ron DeSantis' administration has ordered the removal of license plate reader cameras from Florida's state roadways, citing privacy concerns over the technology. The cameras, manufactured by Flock Safety and other vendors, use artificial intelligence to track vehicle movements and identify suspected violators. The decision marks a reversal…
item.content:encoded:
Governor Ron DeSantis' administration has ordered the removal of license plate reader cameras from Florida's state roadways, citing privacy concerns over the technology. The cameras, manufactured by Flock Safety and other vendors, use artificial intelligence to track vehicle movements and identify suspected violators.

The decision marks a reversal on the surveillance technology that had become increasingly common on state highways. The cameras capture and store license plate data, which privacy advocates have argued raises concerns about government tracking of citizens' movements.

According to reporting on the directive, the administration determined the privacy implications of the widespread deployment outweighed the law enforcement benefits of the camera systems. The move reflects broader national debate over automated license plate readers and the balance between public safety and individual privacy rights.

The removal is expected to proceed across Florida's state road system, though local jurisdictions and municipal police departments may continue using the technology on roads under their control.

item.content:encoded:
A slight chance of showers and thunderstorms is expected this afternoon across the North Escambia area, with only a 20 percent probability of measurable precipitation, according to the National Weather Service forecast.

Tuesday will remain mostly sunny with highs climbing near 91 degrees. Winds will stay calm through the morning before turning northeast around 5 mph in the afternoon.

Looking ahead, meteorologists expect rain chances to increase noticeably as the work week progresses into Friday, so residents should monitor the forecast if outdoor plans are in the works.

item.content:encoded:
A homeless woman has been arrested in connection with an August shooting inside a Cantonment shed, according to the Escambia County Sheriff's Office. Lisa Ann Elliott, 36, was booked into the Escambia County Jail on charges of attempted second-degree murder and shooting into a building. She was being held without bond.

Elliott had been wanted in the case since the August incident. The arrest marks a significant development in what authorities investigated as a serious violent crime in the unincorporated area north of Pensacola.

Details about what led to the shooting or information about any victims have not been released by the Sheriff's Office.

item.title: K-9 Alert Leads to $5K Fentanyl Seizure at I-10 Ag Station
item.dc:creator: newsroom
item.description: A New York truck driver was arrested after law enforcement discovered an estimated $5,000 worth of suspected fentanyl during a routine agricultural inspection at an I-10 inspection station in Escambia County near the state line. According to North Escambia, the fentanyl was intercepted when a K-9 unit alerted officers during the standard ag check.…
item.content:encoded:
A New York truck driver was arrested after law enforcement discovered an estimated $5,000 worth of suspected fentanyl during a routine agricultural inspection at an I-10 inspection station in Escambia County near the state line.

According to North Escambia, the fentanyl was intercepted when a K-9 unit alerted officers during the standard ag check. The seizure highlights the ongoing drug interdiction efforts at critical transportation chokepoints in Northwest Florida.

The arrest marks another successful operation at the agricultural inspection station, which serves as a checkpoint for commercial vehicles entering Escambia County from Georgia. No additional details about the driver's charges or identity have been released.
